final_proof:
**Setup.** Let $|\cdot|_p$ be the $p$-adic norm on $\mathbb{Q}$: $|0|_p=0$ and $|p^k a/b|_p=p^{-k}$ for integers $a,b$ not divisible by $p$. $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is the completion of $(\mathbb{Q},|\cdot|_p)$: the set of Cauchy sequences in $(\mathbb Q,|\cdot|_p)$ modulo the equivalence $(x_N)\sim(y_N)\iff |x_N-y_N|_p\to 0$.

**Step 1 (Cauchy sequences from binary sequences).** For $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_n)_{n\ge0}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ put $s_N(\varepsilon)=\sum_{n=0}^N\varepsilon_n p^n\in\mathbb Z$. For $M>N$, $s_M-s_N=\sum_{n=N+1}^M\varepsilon_np^n$ is divisible by $p^{N+1}$, so $|s_M-s_N|_p\le p^{-(N+1)}\to0$. Hence $(s_N(\varepsilon))_N$ is Cauchy and defines $f(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb Q_p$.

**Step 2 ($f$ is injective).** Let $\varepsilon\ne\delta$ and $k$ the least index with $\varepsilon_k\ne\delta_k$ (the set of such indices is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, so $k$ exists). For $N\ge k$,
$s_N(\varepsilon)-s_N(\delta)=p^k\big((\varepsilon_k-\delta_k)+p\,m_N\big)$ with $m_N=\sum_{n=k+1}^N(\varepsilon_n-\delta_n)p^{n-k-1}\in\mathbb Z$. Since $\varepsilon_k-\delta_k=\pm1$ and $p\ge2$, the integer $\pm1+pm_N$ is not divisible by $p$ (it is $\equiv\pm1\pmod p$), so $|s_N(\varepsilon)-s_N(\delta)|_p=p^{-k}$ for all $N\ge k$. This does not tend to $0$, so the two sequences are not equivalent: $f(\varepsilon)\ne f(\delta)$.

**Step 3 ($\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ is uncountable).** Cantor: for any $g:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ define $\eta_n=1-g(n)_n$. Then $\eta\ne g(n)$ for every $n$ (they differ at coordinate $n$), so no map $\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ is surjective.

**Step 4 (conclusion).** Suppose $\mathbb Q_p$ were countable, i.e. there is an injection $h:\mathbb Q_p\to\mathbb N$. Then $h\circ f:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\to\mathbb N$ is injective with nonempty image $I$. Fix $\varepsilon_0\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ and define $g:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ by $g(i)=(h\circ f)^{-1}(i)$ for $i\in I$ and $g(i)=\varepsilon_0$ otherwise. $g$ is surjective, contradicting Step 3. Hence $\mathbb Q_p$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$

(Remark: if $\mathbb Q_p$ is instead defined as formal series $\sum_{n\ge m}a_np^n$ with digits $a_n\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}$, the map $\varepsilon\mapsto\sum_{n\ge0}\varepsilon_np^n$ is visibly injective, and Steps 3–4 apply verbatim.)
